summary: How the hypothalamus, pituitary, and gonads talk to each other through GnRH, LH, FSH, sex steroids, inhibin, and prolactin. The exam asks you to predict hormone levels when one link in the axis is changed, from a GnRH analog to a prolactinoma to a shift in SHBG.

points: Arcuate nucleus neurons release GnRH in pulses about every 1 to 2 hours into the hypophyseal portal blood.
Each pulse makes gonadotrophs release LH and FSH; faster pulses favor LH, slower pulses favor FSH.
Continuous GnRH (or a long-acting analog such as leuprolide) gives a brief flare, then receptor downregulation, so LH, FSH, and sex steroids fall.
This is why GnRH analogs given continuously treat prostate cancer, endometriosis, and central precocious puberty, while pulsatile pump dosing induces ovulation.
LH acts on Leydig cells to make testosterone.
FSH acts on Sertoli cells to make androgen-binding protein (keeps intratesticular testosterone high), inhibin B, and aromatase.
Testosterone feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary mainly to lower LH.
Inhibin B feeds back on the pituitary to lower FSH selectively.
Exogenous testosterone suppresses LH and FSH, so intratesticular testosterone falls and the testes shrink with low sperm counts.
LH acts on theca cells, which turn cholesterol into androstenedione.
Androstenedione diffuses to granulosa cells, where FSH-induced aromatase turns it into estradiol.
Low to moderate estradiol gives negative feedback on LH and FSH.
Estradiol held above about 200 pg/mL for about 2 days flips to positive feedback and triggers the midcycle LH surge.
Ovulation follows about 34 to 36 hours after the surge begins; the corpus luteum then secretes progesterone, estradiol, and inhibin A.
Testosterone circulates about 1 to 2% free, about 30 to 50% weakly bound to albumin, and the rest tightly bound to SHBG.
Free plus albumin-bound hormone is the bioavailable fraction that reaches tissues.
SHBG rises with estrogen (pregnancy, oral contraceptives), hyperthyroidism, and cirrhosis.
SHBG falls with androgens, insulin resistance (high insulin), obesity, and hypothyroidism.
Low SHBG raises free testosterone even when total testosterone is normal, as in PCOS with hirsutism.
DHT: external genitalia in the fetus, prostate growth, and male-pattern hair loss.
Testosterone: Wolffian duct development, spermatogenesis, muscle mass, libido, and voice deepening.
Estrogen: proliferative endometrium, breast duct growth, thin stretchy cervical mucus, epiphyseal closure, bone preservation, and higher hepatic binding proteins.
Progesterone: secretory endometrium, thick cervical mucus, quiet myometrium, breast lobule development, and a basal body temperature rise of about 0.3 to 0.5 °C (0.5 to 0.9 °F).
Puberty starts when the GnRH pulse generator reactivates after childhood quiescence (kisspeptin signaling helps drive it).
The first sign in the lab is LH pulses during sleep, which later spread across the whole day.
Usual female sequence: thelarche, pubarche, growth spurt, menarche (menarche comes about 2 to 3 years after breast budding).
In boys, testicular enlargement comes first, and the growth spurt comes later than in girls.
Dopamine from the hypothalamus tonically inhibits lactotrophs through D2 receptors; TRH and estrogen stimulate them.
Anything that cuts dopamine (stalk compression, D2 blocking drugs) raises prolactin.
High prolactin suppresses GnRH pulses, so LH, FSH, and sex steroids fall.
Result in women: amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility; in men: low libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility.
Primary hypothyroidism raises TRH, which can raise prolactin.

rows: Gonadotrophs; releases LH and FSH when pulsatile
Inhibited by sex steroids and prolactin
Leydig and theca cells make androgen; triggers ovulation; supports corpus luteum
Lowered by testosterone; surge triggered by sustained high estradiol
Sertoli cells (ABP, inhibin B); granulosa cells (aromatase, follicle growth)
Lowered by inhibin and sex steroids

tricks.label: L for Leydig, L for LH
tricks.text: LH goes to Leydig cells; FSH goes to Sertoli cells, which nurse sperm and make inhibin.

tricks.label: Pulse or pause
tricks.text: Pulsatile GnRH turns the axis on; a steady GnRH signal turns it off. If a drug gives GnRH continuously, expect low LH, FSH, and sex steroids.

tricks.label: Breasts, hair, height, period
tricks.text: The usual order of female puberty: thelarche, pubarche, growth spurt, then menarche.

highYield: Continuous leuprolide suppresses LH and FSH after a short flare; pulsatile GnRH stimulates them.
Inhibin B selectively suppresses FSH; testosterone mainly suppresses LH.
Theca cells (LH) make androgens; granulosa cells (FSH, aromatase) convert them to estradiol.
Sustained high estradiol switches feedback from negative to positive and triggers the LH surge.
Insulin resistance and obesity lower SHBG and raise free testosterone; estrogen raises SHBG.
Hyperprolactinemia causes amenorrhea and galactorrhea by suppressing GnRH pulses.
Puberty begins with sleep-associated LH pulses.
pitfalls: Total testosterone can look normal while free testosterone is high; check SHBG in suspected androgen excess.
Exogenous testosterone raises serum testosterone but lowers intratesticular testosterone and sperm production.
DHT builds the external genitalia and prostate; testosterone builds the Wolffian ducts. Do not swap them.
A GnRH analog first raises LH and FSH (flare) before suppressing them; timing in the stem matters.

dumps.p: Draw one theca cell and one granulosa cell side by side. Show which gonadotropin acts on each, the steroid each makes, and how the cells cooperate to make estradiol.

Theca cell converts cholesterol to androstenedione
Androstenedione diffuses to granulosa cell
FSH receptor on granulosa cell induces aromatase
Aromatase converts androgen to estradiol
Sustained high estradiol switches to positive feedback and LH surge
Granulosa cells also make inhibin B

dumps.p: Draw the hypothalamus, pituitary, Leydig cell, and Sertoli cell. Add arrows for GnRH, LH, FSH, testosterone, ABP, and inhibin B, and mark each feedback loop.
l: Pulsatile GnRH to anterior pituitary
LH to Leydig cell, which makes testosterone
FSH to Sertoli cell, which makes ABP and inhibin B
ABP keeps testosterone high in the seminiferous tubule
Testosterone inhibits GnRH and LH
Inhibin B inhibits FSH
Exogenous testosterone shuts down LH and FSH and shrinks the testes

summary: The enzyme steps that turn cholesterol into progesterone, androgens, and estrogens, and what happens when one step is missing, overactive in fat, or not cleared by the liver. It also covers the glycoprotein hormones and the chemistry of semen, which the exam links to molar pregnancy and PSA.

points: StAR moves cholesterol into the inner mitochondrial membrane (the rate-limiting step).
Cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme (CYP11A1, desmolase) makes pregnenolone; LH stimulates this step through cAMP.
3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase turns pregnenolone into progesterone.
17-alpha-hydroxylase then 17,20-lyase (both on CYP17) turn pregnenolone into DHEA, which 3-beta-HSD turns into androstenedione.
17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase turns androstenedione into testosterone.
Aromatase turns testosterone into estradiol and androstenedione into estrone.
5-alpha-reductase (type 2) converts testosterone to the more potent DHT in genital skin and prostate.
5-alpha-reductase deficiency is autosomal recessive in 46,XY individuals with normal testes.
At birth: ambiguous or female-appearing external genitalia, while Wolffian ducts are normal (testosterone-driven) and Mullerian ducts are absent (AMH present).
At puberty: the testosterone surge virilizes the body (phallic growth, muscle, deep voice), but the prostate stays small and facial hair is sparse.
Labs: normal or high testosterone, low DHT, high testosterone to DHT ratio.
Adipose tissue aromatase converts androstenedione (from adrenal and ovary) to estrone.
After menopause, this peripheral estrone is the main estrogen.
In obesity, more fat means more estrone without matching progesterone (unopposed estrogen).
Unopposed estrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia and endometrioid endometrial carcinoma.
In men, obesity raises estrogen and causes gynecomastia, and the extra estrogen lowers LH and testosterone.
hCG, LH, FSH, and TSH share an identical alpha subunit; the beta subunit gives each its specific action.
Pregnancy tests and tumor markers measure beta-hCG for that reason.
hCG beta closely resembles LH beta, so hCG acts on LH receptors and keeps the corpus luteum alive.
Very high hCG in a hydatidiform mole or choriocarcinoma weakly stimulates TSH receptors, giving hyperthyroidism with low TSH.
Very high hCG also overstimulates the ovaries and causes theca lutein cysts.
The liver inactivates sex steroids, then conjugates them to glucuronides and sulfates for excretion in urine and bile.
Cirrhosis slows estrogen clearance and diverts adrenal androgens around the liver to fat, where they are aromatized.
Cirrhosis also raises SHBG, which binds testosterone more tightly than estradiol, so free estrogen rises relative to free testosterone.
Result: gynecomastia, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, testicular atrophy, and loss of male hair pattern.
Seminal vesicles make most of the volume: fructose (sperm fuel), prostaglandins, and semenogelin that forms the coagulum.
Prostate adds a thin fluid with PSA, citrate, zinc, and acid phosphatase.
PSA is a serine protease (kallikrein) that liquefies the coagulum within about 15 to 30 minutes.
PSA marks prostate tissue of any kind: it rises in BPH (more tissue), prostatitis (leaky inflamed epithelium), and carcinoma.
Absent fructose with low volume points to absent vas deferens or seminal vesicles, or ejaculatory duct obstruction.

charts.title: Steroid enzymes and what loss of each does
rows: Almost no steroids made (lipoid adrenal hyperplasia)
Pregnenolone to progesterone; DHEA to androstenedione
Low cortisol, aldosterone, and potent sex steroids
No sex steroids or cortisol; excess mineralocorticoid with hypertension and low potassium; 46,XY undervirilized
Maternal and fetal virilization; tall stature from open epiphyses
Ambiguous genitalia at birth, virilization at puberty

tricks.label: Read the enzyme name
tricks.text: Each enzyme name tells you where it acts on the steroid ring: 17-alpha-hydroxylase adds an OH at carbon 17, 17,20-lyase cuts between carbons 17 and 20, and 17-beta-HSD changes the group at carbon 17.

tricks.label: Shared alpha, special beta
tricks.text: Four glycoprotein hormones share one alpha chain. When hCG is huge, it starts acting like its relatives LH and TSH.

tricks.label: Virilized at puberty
tricks.text: In 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, a child raised as a girl virilizes at puberty because the large pubertal rise in testosterone (helped by some type 1 5-alpha-reductase in skin) is enough to drive most of the change.

highYield: StAR-mediated cholesterol transfer into mitochondria is the rate-limiting step in steroidogenesis.
Aromatase converts testosterone to estradiol and androstenedione to estrone.
5-alpha-reductase deficiency: 46,XY, ambiguous genitalia at birth, virilization at puberty, high testosterone to DHT ratio.
Obesity and anovulation give unopposed estrogen and endometrial hyperplasia.
Molar pregnancy with very high hCG can cause hyperthyroidism through the TSH receptor.
Cirrhosis causes hyperestrogenism: gynecomastia, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, testicular atrophy.
PSA liquefies semen and rises in BPH and prostatitis as well as cancer; fructose comes from the seminal vesicles.
pitfalls: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency keeps normal Wolffian structures; androgen insensitivity has absent Wolffian structures and female external genitalia with breast development.
After menopause, the main estrogen is estrone made in fat; ovarian estradiol output has largely stopped.
A high PSA alone does not mean cancer; prostatitis and BPH raise it too.
The alpha subunit is shared; lab tests for pregnancy and trophoblastic tumors use beta-hCG.

dumps.p: Starting from cholesterol, draw the pathway to progesterone, DHEA, androstenedione, testosterone, DHT, estrone, and estradiol. Label every enzyme on its arrow.
l: StAR delivers cholesterol into mitochondria (rate-limiting)
Side-chain cleavage makes pregnenolone
3-beta-HSD makes progesterone and androstenedione
17-alpha-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase lead to DHEA
17-beta-HSD makes testosterone (and estradiol from estrone)
Aromatase makes estradiol from testosterone and estrone from androstenedione
5-alpha-reductase makes DHT from testosterone

dumps.p: A man with alcoholic cirrhosis has gynecomastia and small testes. Make a flowchart from liver failure to each of his findings.
l: Less hepatic inactivation and conjugation of estrogen
Portosystemic shunting sends adrenal androstenedione to fat
More peripheral aromatization to estrone
Higher SHBG binds testosterone more than estradiol
Higher free estrogen to free testosterone ratio
Gynecomastia, spider angiomas, palmar erythema
Estrogen lowers LH, so testicular atrophy follows

summary: The nutrients and metabolic fuels that reproduction depends on: folate and iron in pregnancy, glucose across the placenta, lactose and antibodies in milk, zinc, vitamin A, energy availability, and the cholesterol supply for steroid hormones. Questions ask you to predict what a deficiency or excess does to the mother, fetus, or gonads.

points: Tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon units for DNA building blocks.
5,10-methylene-THF gives a methyl group so thymidylate synthase can turn dUMP into dTMP.
N10-formyl-THF supplies two carbons of the purine ring.
Low folate slows DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing neuroepithelium.
The neural tube closes by about day 28 after conception, often before pregnancy is recognized, so supplements must start before conception.
Standard dose is 0.4 mg daily; higher doses are used after a prior affected pregnancy. Folate antagonists and valproate raise risk.
Pregnancy needs about 1 g of extra iron: red cell mass expansion, fetus and placenta, and blood loss at delivery.
Plasma volume rises more (about 40 to 50%) than red cell mass (about 20 to 30%), so hemoglobin falls by dilution.
Dilutional anemia: normal MCV and normal ferritin.
Iron deficiency: low ferritin (below about 30 ng/mL), then low MCV and high RDW.
TIBC rises in normal pregnancy because estrogen raises transferrin, so TIBC alone cannot diagnose iron deficiency here.
Lactose synthase is galactosyltransferase plus alpha-lactalbumin; alpha-lactalbumin switches the acceptor to glucose.
UDP-galactose plus glucose makes lactose, the main osmole that draws water into milk and sets milk volume.
Human milk has more lactose and less total protein than cow milk, with whey proteins making up most of the protein.
It carries secretory IgA, lactoferrin, and lysozyme for gut defense.
It is low in vitamin D (breastfed infants get supplements) and vitamin K (all newborns get vitamin K at birth).
Glucose crosses by facilitated diffusion on GLUT1, down the gradient from mother to fetus.
Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta.
Maternal hyperglycemia means fetal hyperglycemia, so fetal beta cells make more insulin.
Fetal insulin is anabolic: macrosomia with fat over the shoulders and trunk (shoulder dystocia risk).
After the cord is cut, glucose supply stops but insulin stays high, so neonatal hypoglycemia follows.
Fetal hyperinsulinemia also delays surfactant production (respiratory distress).
Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes and for zinc finger transcription factors, including steroid receptors.
Zinc deficiency: hypogonadism, delayed sexual maturation, growth failure, poor wound healing, loss of taste, and periorificial dermatitis.
Excess preformed vitamin A and retinoids such as isotretinoin act on retinoic acid receptors and disrupt neural crest and Hox patterning.
Retinoid embryopathy: craniofacial defects (small or absent ears, cleft palate), conotruncal heart defects, and CNS defects.
Leptin from fat signals to the hypothalamus that energy stores are adequate.
Low energy availability (athletes, eating disorders, very low body fat) lowers leptin and GnRH pulsatility.
LH, FSH, and estradiol fall, causing hypothalamic amenorrhea.
Low estrogen speeds bone resorption, so bone density falls and stress fractures rise.
Gonads and placenta get most cholesterol from circulating LDL by LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis.
LH raises LDL receptor and StAR activity in Leydig and theca cells.
StAR moving cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane is the rate-limiting step in gonadal steroidogenesis.
The placenta makes progesterone from maternal LDL cholesterol but lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase, so it needs fetal adrenal DHEA-S (16-hydroxylated in fetal liver) to make estriol.

charts.title: Anemia in pregnancy
rows: Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass
Iron demand exceeds intake and stores

tricks.label: Sugar crosses, insulin stays
tricks.text: Glucose goes through the placenta, insulin does not. So the fetus answers the mother's sugar with its own insulin, grows big, and crashes after birth.

tricks.label: Ferritin decides
tricks.text: In a pregnant patient with low hemoglobin, look at ferritin and MCV. Normal means dilution; low means iron deficiency.

tricks.label: No fuel, no pulse
tricks.text: When the brain senses low fuel (low leptin), it slows GnRH pulses and periods stop.

highYield: Folate is needed for thymidylate and purine synthesis; neural tube closes by about day 28.
Physiologic anemia of pregnancy has normal MCV and ferritin; iron deficiency has low ferritin.
Lactose synthase = galactosyltransferase plus alpha-lactalbumin.
Breast milk is low in vitamin D and vitamin K.
Maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperinsulinemia, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.
Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen; zinc deficiency causes hypogonadism.
Low leptin from low energy availability suppresses GnRH and causes amenorrhea with bone loss.
StAR is the rate-limiting step; gonads use LDL cholesterol.
pitfalls: Insulin does not cross the placenta; macrosomia comes from fetal insulin.
A raised TIBC is normal in pregnancy; use ferritin to diagnose iron deficiency.
Beta-carotene is not teratogenic; preformed vitamin A in large doses and retinoid drugs are.
HMG-CoA reductase makes cholesterol, but the gonads rely mainly on LDL uptake; the rate-limiting step for steroids is StAR.

dumps.p: Make a flowchart from maternal hyperglycemia to every fetal and newborn consequence. Show what crosses the placenta and what does not.
l: Glucose crosses by facilitated diffusion (GLUT1)
Maternal insulin does not cross
Fetal hyperglycemia stimulates fetal beta cells
Fetal hyperinsulinemia drives macrosomia
Shoulder dystocia risk from shoulder and trunk fat
Delayed surfactant production
Neonatal hypoglycemia after the cord is clamped

dumps.p: Build a table comparing physiologic anemia of pregnancy with iron deficiency anemia. Include the cause and the hemoglobin, MCV, ferritin, RDW, and TIBC findings.
l: Plasma volume rises about 40 to 50%, red cell mass about 20 to 30%
Dilutional: normal MCV
Dilutional: normal ferritin
Iron deficiency: low ferritin first
Iron deficiency: low MCV and high RDW
TIBC rises in normal pregnancy, so it does not separate the two
Total iron need is about 1 g

summary: How chromosome errors and gene mutations cause reproductive disease: sex chromosome aneuploidy, X inactivation, HPV oncoproteins, and the inherited breast, ovarian, and endometrial cancer syndromes. The exam asks you to connect a karyotype or mutation to its mechanism and phenotype.

points: Meiosis I nondisjunction: homologous chromosomes fail to separate.
Meiosis II nondisjunction: sister chromatids fail to separate.
47,XXY (Klinefelter): extra X from either parent; about half of cases come from the father (an XY sperm).
45,X (Turner): usually the lost sex chromosome is paternal, and risk does not rise with maternal age.
Nondisjunction or chromosome loss after fertilization gives mosaicism (for example 45,X/46,XX) with milder features.
45,X/46,XY mosaics carry gonadoblastoma risk in their dysgenetic gonads.
XIST, a long noncoding RNA, coats one X in cis and silences it, forming the Barr body.
Inactivation is random in each cell early in the embryo and then fixed in its descendants.
Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes minus one: 46,XX has 1, 47,XXY has 1, 45,X has 0, 47,XXX has 2.
Some genes (including pseudoautosomal SHOX) escape inactivation, which is why 45,X and 47,XXY still have phenotypes.
Klinefelter: tall, small firm testes, azoospermia, gynecomastia, low testosterone with high LH and FSH.
Klinefelter testes show hyalinized seminiferous tubules and low inhibin B; male breast cancer risk rises.
Turner: short stature (SHOX loss), streak ovaries, primary amenorrhea, high FSH and LH, low estrogen.
Turner also: webbed neck and lymphedema (from cystic hygroma), bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, and horseshoe kidney.
High-risk HPV (16, 18) DNA often integrates into host DNA, disrupting E2, the gene that normally restrains E6 and E7.
E6 binds p53 and recruits a ubiquitin ligase, so p53 is degraded and damaged cells neither arrest nor die.
E7 binds Rb and releases E2F, which pushes the cell from G1 into S phase.
Loss of both checkpoints lets mutations pile up in the cervical transformation zone; p16 staining rises as a marker.
BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressors that repair double-strand breaks by homologous recombination.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant; a tumor forms after the second allele is lost (two-hit).
BRCA1: breast and high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma; breast tumors are often triple-negative basal-like.
BRCA2: breast, ovarian, male breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancer.
Lynch syndrome: autosomal dominant germline mismatch repair mutations (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) with microsatellite instability.
In women with Lynch, endometrial carcinoma risk is as high as or higher than colorectal risk; ovarian risk also rises.
Luminal A: ER and PR positive, HER2 negative, low proliferation, best prognosis, responds to hormone therapy.
Luminal B: ER positive with higher proliferation, with or without HER2.
HER2-enriched: ERBB2 gene amplification, ER negative, responds to HER2-targeted antibody therapy.
Basal-like: ER, PR, and HER2 negative (triple-negative), high grade, younger patients, linked to BRCA1.

charts.title: Inherited reproductive cancer genes
rows: Breast (female and male), ovarian, prostate, pancreatic
Not inherited here; E6 causes p53 protein degradation
Cervical carcinoma (with E7 action on Rb)

tricks.label: Count Xs, subtract one
tricks.text: Barr bodies always equal the number of X chromosomes minus one, no matter how many Y chromosomes there are.

tricks.label: E6 for p53, E7 for Rb
tricks.text: Pair them in order: E6 with p53 and E7 with Rb. The smaller E number goes with the protein that comes first in the alphabet (p before R).

tricks.label: BRCA2 reaches men
tricks.text: Male breast cancer and prostate cancer in a family point to BRCA2 more than BRCA1.

highYield: Postzygotic nondisjunction gives mosaicism with a milder phenotype.
XIST silences one X; Barr bodies = X count minus one.
HPV E6 degrades p53; E7 inactivates Rb and frees E2F.
BRCA1 and BRCA2 repair double-strand breaks by homologous recombination; both are autosomal dominant.
BRCA1 tumors are often triple-negative basal-like; BRCA2 adds male breast and prostate cancer.
Lynch syndrome: mismatch repair loss, microsatellite instability, endometrial and colorectal cancer.
HER2-positive breast cancer comes from ERBB2 gene amplification.
pitfalls: 45,X usually results from loss of the paternal sex chromosome and is not tied to maternal age.
Klinefelter (47,XXY) has a Barr body; Turner (45,X) does not.
Triple-negative means ER, PR, and HER2 negative; it does not respond to hormone or HER2-targeted therapy.
Microsatellite instability with loss of MLH1 can be sporadic (promoter hypermethylation) as well as inherited; germline testing separates them.

dumps.p: Draw meiosis I and meiosis II for the sex chromosomes in a father. Show how nondisjunction in each division can produce 47,XXY or 45,X offspring.
l: Meiosis I separates homologs (X from Y)
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids
Meiosis I error in the father gives an XY sperm
XY sperm plus X egg gives 47,XXY
A sperm with no sex chromosome plus an X egg gives 45,X
Error after fertilization gives mosaicism
Mosaics have milder features

dumps.p: Draw the G1 to S checkpoint with p53, p21, cyclin-CDK, Rb, and E2F. Then show where HPV E6 and E7 act.
l: DNA damage activates p53
p53 induces p21, which inhibits cyclin-CDK
Unphosphorylated Rb holds E2F
Phosphorylated Rb releases E2F to start S phase
E6 targets p53 for ubiquitin-mediated degradation
E7 binds Rb and releases E2F
High-risk types 16 and 18 integrate and overexpress E6 and E7

summary: How the immune system behaves in the reproductive tract: protecting sperm and the fetus from attack, passing antibodies to the newborn, guarding the vagina, and causing damage in Rh disease and tubal infection. The exam asks you to link an immune mechanism to a clinical outcome such as infertility, hydrops, or ectopic pregnancy.

points: Sperm antigens appear at puberty, long after self-tolerance forms, so they look foreign.
Sertoli cell tight junctions form the blood-testis barrier and hide meiotic and postmeiotic germ cells.
Local immunosuppression adds protection: TGF-beta, Fas ligand, anti-inflammatory macrophages, and regulatory T cells.
Barrier breach (trauma, torsion, vasectomy, mumps orchitis) exposes sperm and leads to antisperm antibodies.
Antisperm antibodies agglutinate sperm and reduce motility, causing infertility.
Autoimmune orchitis (alone or in autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes) destroys the testis, causing primary hypogonadism with high LH and FSH.
The fetus carries paternal antigens, so it is a semiallogeneic graft.
Trophoblast in contact with maternal blood lacks classical HLA-A and HLA-B, so maternal cytotoxic T cells have little to recognize.
Extravillous trophoblast expresses nonclassical HLA-G, which binds inhibitory receptors on uterine NK cells and T cells.
HLA-G prevents NK cells from attacking the cells for missing class I (the missing-self signal).
Complement regulators on trophoblast and expanded maternal regulatory T cells add more protection.
Maternal IgG crosses the placenta by FcRn-mediated transcytosis, mostly in the third trimester.
IgM is a large pentamer that does not bind FcRn, so it does not cross.
IgM in cord blood was made by the fetus and signals congenital infection.
Maternal IgG wanes over about 6 months, so preterm infants and infants at 3 to 6 months are most vulnerable.
Breast milk secretory IgA coats the infant gut and blocks pathogen attachment; colostrum has the most.
An RhD-negative mother is exposed to RhD-positive fetal red cells by fetomaternal hemorrhage, usually at delivery.
Sensitization usually happens at the first delivery and the first response is mostly IgM, so the first baby is usually spared.
In a later RhD-positive pregnancy, memory B cells make anti-D IgG that crosses the placenta.
IgG-coated fetal red cells are destroyed by splenic macrophages (type II hypersensitivity).
Fetal anemia leads to extramedullary hematopoiesis, hepatosplenomegaly, high-output heart failure, and hydrops fetalis.
After birth, unconjugated bilirubin rises fast and can cause kernicterus.
Anti-D immune globulin at about 28 weeks and after delivery or any bleeding event clears fetal cells before the mother is sensitized.
Estrogen loads vaginal epithelium with glycogen, which lactobacilli ferment to lactic acid, keeping the pH at or below 4.5; some also make hydrogen peroxide.
Secretory IgA and antimicrobial peptides add mucosal protection.
When lactobacilli are lost (douching, antibiotics, new partners), Gardnerella and anaerobes overgrow: bacterial vaginosis with pH above 4.5 and fishy amines.
The vaccine is L1 capsid protein that self-assembles into virus-like particles with no viral DNA.
It induces neutralizing IgG that blocks infection; it does not treat existing infection or lesions.
Most natural HPV infections and low-grade lesions are cleared by cell-mediated immunity within about 2 years.
Low CD4 counts (HIV, transplant immunosuppression) let HPV persist, so CIN and cervical cancer rise.
Chlamydia and gonorrhea ascend from the cervix to the tubes (salpingitis, PID).
Chlamydia is often silent, so infections go untreated and recur; repeat exposure drives stronger T cell-mediated inflammation.
Gonococcal lipooligosaccharide and peptidoglycan trigger TNF release that kills ciliated cells.
Healing causes fibrosis, loss of cilia, adhesions, and blocked tubes (hydrosalpinx).
Partial damage traps the embryo, causing ectopic pregnancy; complete blockage causes tubal factor infertility.

charts.title: Immune protection of the fetus and newborn
rows: Fetus survives as a semiallogeneic graft
Inhibits uterine NK cells and T cells
Also carries harmful IgG (anti-D, maternal autoantibodies)
Fetal IgM is the fetus's own
Fewer infant GI and respiratory infections

charts.title: Immune damage in the reproductive tract
rows: Autoimmunity, alone or with polyendocrine syndrome

tricks.label: G for Gestation
tricks.text: HLA-G is the gestation HLA: it sits on trophoblast and tells maternal NK cells to stand down.

tricks.label: IgG goes, IgM stays
tricks.text: G for gets across. IgM is too big to cross, so any IgM found in the newborn was made by the newborn.

tricks.label: First baby fine, second baby sick
tricks.text: Rh disease needs prior sensitization and a class switch to IgG, so problems show up in a later Rh-positive pregnancy.

highYield: The blood-testis barrier is formed by Sertoli cell tight junctions; breach leads to antisperm antibodies.
Trophoblast expresses HLA-G and lacks HLA-A and HLA-B.
IgG crosses the placenta by FcRn; IgM does not; secretory IgA comes in breast milk.
Rh disease is type II hypersensitivity by maternal anti-D IgG; anti-D immune globulin prevents sensitization.
Lactobacilli keep vaginal pH at or below 4.5; their loss allows bacterial vaginosis.
HPV vaccine is L1 virus-like particles that induce neutralizing antibodies.
HIV raises cervical cancer risk because T cell clearance of HPV fails.
Repeated chlamydial and gonococcal salpingitis scar the tubes, causing ectopic pregnancy and infertility.
pitfalls: Rh disease is type II hypersensitivity (IgG against a red cell surface antigen); there are no immune complexes.
The HPV vaccine prevents infection; it does not clear an established lesion.
ABO incompatibility can affect a first pregnancy and is usually milder than Rh disease.
Mumps orchitis is usually unilateral, so complete sterility is uncommon.

dumps.p: Draw two pregnancies in an RhD-negative mother with RhD-positive babies. Show sensitization in the first, the attack in the second, and where anti-D immune globulin would prevent it.
l: Fetomaternal hemorrhage at first delivery
Primary response is mainly IgM, which does not cross
Memory B cells form
Second pregnancy: anti-D IgG crosses by FcRn
Type II hypersensitivity: splenic destruction of fetal red cells
Fetal anemia leads to hydrops fetalis
Anti-D immune globulin at about 28 weeks and after delivery

dumps.p: Make a flowchart from a silent chlamydial cervicitis to an ectopic pregnancy years later. Name the immune steps.
l: Asymptomatic infection goes untreated
Ascent to the fallopian tube (salpingitis)
Repeated infection drives stronger T cell-mediated inflammation
Loss of ciliated cells
Fibrosis and adhesions narrow the tube
Embryo transport is slowed and implants in the tube
Complete blockage instead causes tubal factor infertility

summary: The organisms behind sexually transmitted and pregnancy-related infections: their structure, how they grow, how they spread, and the lab features that identify them. The exam gives a smear, culture, or virulence factor and asks you to name the organism or explain how it causes disease.

points: Gram-negative diplococcus, oxidase positive, ferments glucose but not maltose (meningococcus ferments both).
Grown on Thayer-Martin agar, a selective chocolate agar with antibiotics that suppress normal flora.
Pili attach to epithelium and undergo antigenic variation, so reinfection is common and no vaccine exists.
IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA; lipooligosaccharide acts as endotoxin; there is no polysaccharide capsule.
Men show intracellular diplococci in neutrophils on Gram stain of urethral discharge; nucleic acid amplification is the usual test.
Obligate intracellular bacterium that depends on host cell ATP.
Elementary body: small, infectious, enters cells by endocytosis.
Reticulate body: replicates by binary fission inside an inclusion, then turns back into elementary bodies that are released.
Cell wall has little peptidoglycan, so beta-lactams do not work well.
Serovars A to C: trachoma; D to K: urethritis, cervicitis, PID, neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia; L1 to L3: lymphogranuloma venereum.
Thin, tightly coiled spirochete with periplasmic flagella; too thin to see on Gram stain.
Seen by dark-field microscopy of chancre fluid; cannot be cultured on standard media.
Spread by sexual contact with lesions and across the placenta.
Diagnosis is mainly serologic: nontreponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) track activity; treponemal tests usually stay positive for life.
HSV-2: enveloped linear dsDNA herpesvirus; painful vesicles that ulcerate.
HSV-2 travels up sensory nerves and stays latent in sacral sensory ganglia, then reactivates as recurrent outbreaks.
HPV: nonenveloped circular dsDNA papillomavirus that infects basal keratinocytes through small breaks in the epithelium.
HPV-infected cells show koilocytes (perinuclear halo, wrinkled nucleus).
Low-risk types 6 and 11: genital warts (condyloma acuminatum). High-risk types 16 and 18: CIN and squamous carcinoma.
Trichomonas vaginalis: motile, pear-shaped flagellated protozoan on saline wet mount; frothy discharge, pH above 4.5.
Candida albicans: budding yeast with pseudohyphae on KOH prep; thick white discharge, pH normal.
Gardnerella vaginalis: clue cells (epithelial cells coated with bacteria) on wet mount; fishy odor with KOH, pH above 4.5, few white cells.
Haemophilus ducreyi: small gram-negative coccobacillus that grows in chains on Gram stain ('school of fish').
Chancroid ulcers are painful with a ragged purulent base and painful suppurative inguinal nodes.
Staphylococcus aureus TSST-1 is a superantigen that links MHC class II to the T cell receptor beta chain outside the antigen groove.
This activates a huge fraction of T cells at once, causing a cytokine storm (IL-2, IFN-gamma, TNF).
Toxic shock: fever, hypotension, diffuse rash with later desquamation, and multiorgan injury, classically with retained tampons or nasal packing.
Streptococcus agalactiae: gram-positive cocci in chains, beta-hemolytic, bacitracin resistant, CAMP positive.
Colonizes the vagina and rectum of many pregnant women; screened by culture at 36 to 37 weeks.
Causes neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis acquired during delivery.
TORCH: Toxoplasma, Other (syphilis, varicella-zoster, parvovirus B19, Listeria, HIV, Zika), Rubella, CMV, HSV.
Most TORCH organisms cross the placenta; HSV is mainly acquired during delivery.

tricks.label: ABC, D to K, L
tricks.text: Chlamydia serovars: A, B, C = Africa, Blindness, Chronic infection (trachoma). D to K = everything else genital and neonatal. L1 to L3 = Lymphogranuloma venereum.

tricks.label: You do cry with ducreyi
tricks.text: Chancroid from Haemophilus ducreyi is painful; the syphilis chancre is painless.

tricks.label: MeninGococci ferment Maltose and Glucose
tricks.text: Meningococcus ferments maltose and glucose; Gonococcus ferments glucose only.

tricks.label: B for Bacitracin resistant, B for Babies
tricks.text: Group B strep is bacitracin resistant and causes disease in babies.

highYield: Gonococcus: oxidase positive, glucose only, Thayer-Martin, pilus antigenic variation means no vaccine.
Chlamydia: elementary body infects, reticulate body replicates; serovars A to C, D to K, L1 to L3.
Treponema pallidum: dark-field microscopy, no routine culture, crosses the placenta.
HSV-2 is enveloped and latent in sacral ganglia; HPV is nonenveloped; types 16 and 18 are high risk.
Clue cells mean Gardnerella; pseudohyphae on KOH mean Candida; motile flagellates mean Trichomonas.
TSST-1 is a superantigen linking MHC II and TCR outside the peptide groove.
Group B strep: beta-hemolytic, bacitracin resistant, CAMP positive; top cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.
pitfalls: Group A strep is bacitracin sensitive; group B is bacitracin resistant.
Candida vaginitis has a normal pH; bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis raise it above 4.5.
Syphilis chancre is painless and indurated; chancroid is painful and soft.
Toxoplasma calcifications are scattered through the brain; CMV calcifications are periventricular.
Superantigens skip antigen processing; they do not need to fit in the MHC peptide groove.

dumps.p: Draw the chlamydial life cycle in a host cell, from entry of the infectious form to release of new infectious particles. Label both forms.
l: Elementary body attaches and enters by endocytosis
Elementary body is small, dense, and infectious
Inside an inclusion, it becomes a reticulate body
Reticulate body divides by binary fission
Reticulate bodies turn back into elementary bodies
Cell ruptures and releases elementary bodies
Obligate intracellular because it depends on host ATP

dumps.p: Build a comparison table of syphilis, chancroid, genital herpes, and lymphogranuloma venereum. Include organism, structure, pain, ulcer appearance, lymph nodes, and lab test.
l: Syphilis: Treponema pallidum spirochete, painless indurated chancre, dark-field or serology
Chancroid: Haemophilus ducreyi coccobacillus, painful ragged ulcer
Chancroid nodes are painful and can suppurate
Herpes: HSV-2, painful grouped vesicles that ulcerate, PCR
Herpes recurs from latency in sacral ganglia
LGV: Chlamydia L1 to L3, small painless ulcer then painful inguinal nodes
Syphilis nodes are painless and rubbery
